HelioFinance (Miguel) to send a minimal repro (Node version, proxy path, and sample logs with request-id) for the streaming disconnect.
Redwood (Dana) to confirm current TS SDK behavior on mid-stream disconnects and whether it retries after first event (and if so, how to disable).

content:
Meeting header
- Date: 2025-01-16
- Time: 10:00 AM PT
- Duration: 47 min
- Call type: Technical deep dive
- Account: HelioFinance
- Redwood: Nikhil Sharma (Product), Ibrahim Khan (DevEx/SDK TL), Dana Lo (TypeScript SDK)
- Customer: Sarah Kim (Staff Eng), Miguel Alvarez (Platform), Priya Natarajan (Security)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Customer is evaluating Redwood streaming in production and sees intermittent disconnects in Node/TypeScript path.
- Customer asked how Redwood SDKs decide what to retry (429/5xx) and whether streaming should auto-retry.
- Redwood described current work to standardize SDK behavior (retries, timeouts, streaming semantics) across Python/TS/Go and reduce retry storms.
- Next steps: share guidance + repro details + follow-up on proxy/SSE buffering.

Topics
1) HelioFinance current architecture (Node workers, reverse proxy, SSE)
2) Observed streaming disconnects + partial frames
3) Retry strategy (429/5xx/transport) and safe behavior for streaming
4) Request IDs, Retry-After, and debugging signals
5) Security notes (API key handling, logging redaction)

Transcript

[00:00] Nikhil Sharma: Cool, thanks everyone for joining. This is Nikhil. I think the goal today is to go a little deeper on the SDK streaming behavior and retries. I’ve got Ibrahim and Dana here.

[00:10] Sarah Kim: Hey, I’m Sarah. Thanks. Yeah, we’re mostly here because we like, we got it working, but then in our staging it… it drops the stream sometimes.

[00:20] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel, platform. We run Node behind an Envoy gateway, then Cloudflare in front for some apps. So we’re trying to figure out whose timeout is killing it.

[00:31] Priya Natarajan: Priya, security. I’m mostly listening, but I do have a question around what headers you require and what gets logged by default.

[00:41] Nikhil Sharma: Great. Ibrahim, do you want to set context on what we’re changing on the SDK side? Like, we’ve been doing a parity pass.

[00:48] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah, sure. So we’re in the middle of a cross-SDK parity audit—Python, TypeScript, Go—specifically around auth resolution, retry defaults, timeout defaults, and streaming semantics. The reason is exactly what you’re seeing: inconsistent behavior leads to weird failure modes.

[01:05] Dana Lo: And streaming is the spiciest one because every runtime treats SSE a little differently. Node fetch vs undici, proxies, partial chunks, etc.

[01:15] Sarah Kim: Okay, so I’ll just describe what we saw. We’re using the TS SDK, we call chat streaming, we pipe tokens to the browser. It’ll work for like 60 seconds, and then we get an error that looks like “socket hang up” or “connection terminated” and we didn’t cancel it.

[01:34] Miguel Alvarez: And the weird part: sometimes we see it reconnect and then we get duplicated tokens, like it restarts from the beginning. Not always, but enough that it’s scary.

[01:45] Dana Lo: Got it. When you say reconnect—are you doing that in your app, or you think the SDK is re-issuing the request?

[01:52] Sarah Kim: We’re not doing it intentionally. We have a generic retry wrapper around HTTP calls for non-streaming, but we disabled it for streaming. So we suspect the SDK maybe?

[02:04] Dana Lo: Okay. Good detail. In our current TS implementation we have a “retry on network errors” layer for some endpoints, and that’s part of what we’re tightening. For streaming specifically, the intended standard is: do not automatically retry once you’ve received any part of the stream body.

[02:22] Ibrahim Khan: Right—because you can’t make it idempotent unless you have server-side resume semantics, which we don’t guarantee.

[02:30] Miguel Alvarez: That’s the main question: what’s your official stance? Like, do you recommend retries on 429 and 503 and whatnot? And how does that work with rate limiting? Because we got burned by retry storms with another provider.

[02:46] Nikhil Sharma: Yeah, makes sense. We can break it into: (1) non-streaming requests: safe retries with a budget and backoff; (2) streaming: conservative.

[02:56] Dana Lo: To answer directly: for streaming responses, we should only retry if we never started reading the body. Like, DNS failure, connect failure, TLS handshake, request timed out before any bytes. Once we have the first SSE event, we treat it as “in progress” and if it disconnects, we surface the error.

[03:15] Sarah Kim: That matches what we want. Today we are not sure if the SDK is doing that.

[03:22] Dana Lo: Understood. We’ll confirm what version you’re on and what the behavior is. What Node version?

[03:29] Sarah Kim: Node 18 in prod, Node 20 in dev. (laughs) which might be part of it.

[03:36] Dana Lo: Not laughing at you—yeah Node 18 vs 20 changes the fetch/undici behavior. Are you using global fetch or a polyfill?

[03:45] Sarah Kim: Global fetch in 18, I think it’s undici under the hood.

[03:50] Miguel Alvarez: We’re also sometimes running in AWS Lambda for some jobs, but the streaming case is mostly k8s.

[03:58] Ibrahim Khan: On timeouts: do you have any idle timeout on Envoy for upstream connections? A 60-second disconnect often screams “idle timeout” or “max stream duration” on a proxy.

[04:10] Miguel Alvarez: Envoy has a 60 second default for some routes, yes. But we turned it up. Cloudflare also has like 100 seconds on something. But we still see it at ~60-70.

[04:22] Sarah Kim: It’s not exact. Sometimes it’s 45 seconds.

[04:26] Dana Lo: In SSE, if there’s a long gap between events, some proxies think it’s idle even though the TCP is alive. One pattern is to send comment frames “:keepalive\n\n” from the server. Do you know if Redwood sends keep-alives?

[04:43] Nikhil Sharma: We do send periodic events in most models, but it depends on token cadence. If the model stalls—like long reasoning before first token—then there can be a gap.

[04:54] Sarah Kim: Yes, exactly. The first token sometimes takes 20-30 seconds, and then it starts flowing.

[05:02] Ibrahim Khan: That fits. So what we typically recommend is:
- Set a higher “time to first byte” tolerance for streaming.
- Avoid aggressive read timeouts.
- Make sure the proxy doesn’t buffer SSE.

[05:16] Miguel Alvarez: The buffering thing—yeah we had that issue once. Envoy buffered and then dumped a big chunk.

[05:23] Dana Lo: And that can break naive SSE parsers because you can get partial frames, or multiple frames at once, or a frame split in the middle of “data:”.

[05:35] Sarah Kim: We did see partial frames in logs. Like it ended with “data: {\”delta\”:” and then boom disconnect.

[05:43] Dana Lo: That’s a classic partial chunk. The parser needs to hold onto the remainder until it gets the delimiter “\n\n”. If the SDK treats partial as an error, that could surface incorrectly. Or if your app logs mid-chunk, it looks like JSON is broken.

[05:58] Sarah Kim: Hmm. We’re logging raw bytes (bad, I know). Just for debugging.

[06:05] Priya Natarajan: Can I jump in? Please don’t log raw headers if your API key is in there. Do your SDKs redact it automatically?

[06:13] Ibrahim Khan: Yes—our secure default posture is: never log the API key, and if we throw an error we also don’t include the key in the message. We also recommend customers avoid logging request headers. On our side, we use an Authorization header with a bearer token.

[06:28] Priya Natarajan: Bearer, okay. Some providers do “X-API-Key”. Just want to know.

[06:33] Nikhil Sharma: We standardize on Authorization: Bearer <key>. The SDK will source it from env vars or config.

[06:40] Priya Natarajan: Great. And request IDs? Like if we open a ticket we can point to a request.

[06:46] Ibrahim Khan: Yes—responses include a request-id header. In some places it’s “x-request-id”; we’re making that consistent. We strongly recommend you log request-id and status code, but not auth.

[07:02] Miguel Alvarez: Okay, so on retries. Let’s say we hit 429. What do you do, and what do you recommend?

[07:10] Ibrahim Khan: Our standard is:
- Retry on 429, and most 5xx (like 500, 502, 503, 504), plus certain transport errors (connection reset, timeout during connect).
- Do exponential backoff with jitter.
- Respect Retry-After if present.
- Enforce a retry budget: max attempts and max total time.

[07:33] Miguel Alvarez: What is “max attempts” in practice?

[07:36] Ibrahim Khan: The exact default varies today across SDKs—that’s what we’re fixing. Target is something like 2-3 retries max by default for non-streaming. Not 10. And we avoid immediate retries.

[07:52] Sarah Kim: And for streaming, you said basically no retries after first chunk.

[07:56] Dana Lo: Correct. One nuance: we might do a single retry on initial connect failure before any body bytes, but not once it starts. And we won’t silently restart a stream because it can duplicate output.

[08:10] Miguel Alvarez: That duplication is what we saw. So if it is the SDK, we want that off.

[08:16] Dana Lo: Yep. We’ll verify. Also, a bunch of folks wrap fetch with something that retries on any network error, and it doesn’t know streaming vs non-streaming. So just flagging: check if Envoy or your client has “retry on reset” policy.

[08:30] Miguel Alvarez: Envoy does have retry on connect-failure for some routes. That could be it too. But that would retry the whole request to you.

[08:38] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. If Envoy retries upstream mid-stream, you’ll get “duplicated tokens” but not because the SDK did it. You’d see two separate request IDs though.

[08:50] Sarah Kim: We saw two request IDs in our logs, yes. That’s interesting.

[08:55] Nikhil Sharma: That’s actually great evidence. If you can share a snippet: timestamps + request IDs, we can correlate on our side.

[09:04] Miguel Alvarez: Okay, we can do that.

[09:08] Dana Lo: Another question: are you streaming from Redwood directly to the browser, or do you terminate at your server and re-stream?

[09:16] Sarah Kim: We terminate at our server. Browser connects to us, we connect to you. We don’t want clients to have keys.

[09:23] Dana Lo: Good. In that setup, you need to make sure your server flushes chunks immediately. Some frameworks buffer writes.

[09:31] Sarah Kim: We’re using Express. We do res.write. But there’s also a compression middleware sometimes.

[09:38] Dana Lo: Compression can absolutely buffer. SSE with gzip can be weird. Try disabling compression on SSE routes.

[09:47] Miguel Alvarez: That might explain the “stall then disconnect” if Cloudflare thinks it’s idle.

[09:52] Ibrahim Khan: Yup. If nothing is flushed, the downstream sees no activity.

[10:00] Nikhil Sharma: Let’s talk about what you want from us, in terms of official guidance. Are you trying to ship this in Q1?

[10:07] Sarah Kim: Ideally February. We need consistent behavior across our services. Some are Python, some are Node.

[10:15] Miguel Alvarez: And we need to make sure retries won’t blow up our rate limit. Some providers punish you if you keep retrying 429.

[10:23] Ibrahim Khan: We’re aligned. Our retry approach is designed to be “polite”: respect Retry-After, add jitter, and cap attempts. Also, we aim to expose hooks so you can override per request.

[10:37] Priya Natarajan: Do you support idempotency keys? Like if we do a non-streaming request and you retry it, we don’t want double billing.

[10:45] Nikhil Sharma: We have idempotency guidance for certain endpoints. For chat generation, idempotency is tricky because output can be nondeterministic. We can still support an Idempotency-Key header for request de-dupe in some cases, but it’s not a guarantee today across all modes.

[11:02] Ibrahim Khan: That’s why the SDK default is conservative and why we don’t retry streaming mid-flight. For non-streaming, the risk is “duplicate completions” more than “double charge”—but I get the concern. We can talk through how we count usage. Typically usage is per successful response; failures don’t charge.

[11:21] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[11:22] Miguel Alvarez: On 429, do you always send Retry-After?

[11:26] Nikhil Sharma: Usually, yes, and we’re improving consistency. But it can depend on the gateway path.

[11:33] Ibrahim Khan: For the SDK standard, the rule is: if Retry-After present, honor it; otherwise use backoff.

[11:41] Dana Lo: Also we classify rate limit errors sometimes with machine-readable error codes. But again, depending on response payload, that’s being standardized.

[11:50] Sarah Kim: We saw a JSON body like { error: { message: … } } but not a code.

[11:56] Dana Lo: Yep, that’s part of the normalization work.

[12:00] Miguel Alvarez: Can we shift back to streaming disconnect. If it disconnects, what do you recommend the application do? Like, should we re-issue the request?

[12:10] Ibrahim Khan: It depends. If you have not delivered any tokens to your end user, you can retry safely-ish. If you already delivered partial output, retrying will create a different continuation, and you’ll need to handle it at the product layer (like showing “connection lost, click to resume”).

[12:27] Dana Lo: There’s no guaranteed resume point. SSE has Last-Event-ID as a concept, but our API doesn’t promise resumable streams. So the safe behavior is: surface an error with context (request-id, bytes received), and let the app decide.

[12:44] Sarah Kim: Okay, so the SDK shouldn’t hide it.

[12:47] Dana Lo: Correct.

[12:50] Miguel Alvarez: One issue: our UI expects the stream to end with a “done” marker. If it disconnects, our UI just spins.

[12:57] Dana Lo: That’s common. You should treat a disconnect as terminal and send your UI an error event. The SDK can provide an “onError” callback.

[13:07] Sarah Kim: Today we just await the iterator and it throws, but our code path doesn’t notify the client.

[13:14] Nikhil Sharma: That’s an app fix we can help with examples. Sabrina from our examples team isn’t on this call but we can share a snippet.

[13:22] Priya Natarajan: Quick question: do you ever include prompts in error logs? We have PII policies.

[13:28] Ibrahim Khan: In the SDK, we do not log prompts by default. We keep logging minimal. If you enable debug logging, we still recommend redacting payload content; we’re adding guardrails there too.

[13:42] Priya Natarajan: Great.

[13:44] Dana Lo: Back to the technicals: can you share your exact code for streaming? Like are you using the SDK’s built-in streaming helper or calling fetch directly?

[13:54] Sarah Kim: SDK helper. It looks like:

[14:00] Sarah Kim: client.chat.completions.stream({ model: ..., messages: ... })

[14:06] Sarah Kim: Then for await (const event of stream) { ... }

[14:12] Dana Lo: Okay. And when it disconnects, what’s the error type?

[14:17] Sarah Kim: It’s not super consistent. Sometimes it’s AbortError, but we didn’t abort. Sometimes it’s “TypeError: fetch failed”.

[14:26] Dana Lo: That can be undici. It throws “TypeError: fetch failed” for a bunch of underlying socket errors.

[14:33] Miguel Alvarez: We also saw “ECONNRESET”.

[14:36] Dana Lo: Yep.

[14:38] Ibrahim Khan: One thing we’re standardizing is error taxonomy: making sure “timeout” vs “cancel” vs “disconnect” are clearly distinct, across languages.

[14:50] Sarah Kim: That would help. Right now support tickets are hard because you can’t tell if it’s user cancel or network.

[14:57] Nikhil Sharma: For sure.

[15:00] Miguel Alvarez: Do you support a client-side timeout for “time to first token”? That’s what we want. Like, if nothing happens for 45 seconds, we want to bail and show a message.

[15:11] Dana Lo: We’ll have a standard timeout config. Typically: connect timeout, overall timeout, and for streaming, a “first byte” timeout or read timeout. But we’re careful because too aggressive will kill legitimate long-first-token cases.

[15:27] Ibrahim Khan: Recommended default for streaming is “no read timeout” or a large one, plus allow user override. But having an app-level “TTFT budget” is reasonable.

[15:38] Sarah Kim: We’d implement that at the product layer.

[15:41] Dana Lo: Exactly. In Node you can use AbortController with a timer to cancel if you want.

[15:49] Miguel Alvarez: But then it looks like user cancel.

[15:52] Dana Lo: We can surface a specific TimeoutError when the abort was due to our timer. That’s part of the standardization.

[16:02] Priya Natarajan: So you’ll have consistent error messages, but not include secrets.

[16:06] Ibrahim Khan: Yep.

[16:08] Nikhil Sharma: Another point: we’ve seen customers run into proxy buffering and also HTTP/2 weirdness. Are you forcing HTTP/2 anywhere?

[16:18] Miguel Alvarez: Cloudflare might do h2 to the browser. Upstream to our service is h1. Then our service to you is h2, I think? Not sure.

[16:27] Sarah Kim: Node fetch will negotiate h2? I don’t know.

[16:30] Dana Lo: undici mostly does h1 for fetch unless configured. But if there’s a corporate proxy or something, it can alter things.

[16:40] Miguel Alvarez: We do have Zscaler for some corporate traffic, but prod servers don’t go through it.

[16:46] Ibrahim Khan: Okay.

[16:48] Sarah Kim: Another symptom: sometimes the stream doesn’t disconnect, but it “freezes” after like 200 tokens. Then 20 seconds later it continues.

[16:58] Dana Lo: That can be model side (stall) or network buffering. If you have compression on your own response, it might flush in bigger chunks.

[17:08] Miguel Alvarez: We do have gzip. We’ll disable it.

[17:12] Nikhil Sharma: Great. That might fix a lot.

[17:15] Ibrahim Khan: If you can capture a timeline like: when you got first event, then when it stalled, plus request-id, we can check our internal logs for whether tokens were produced continuously.

[17:28] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[17:30] Miguel Alvarez: Switching gears—if we adopt Redwood across services, we need consistent behavior between Python and TS. Our Python service uses httpx, and it retries a bit differently.

[17:41] Ibrahim Khan: Yep, that’s part of the parity work. The end state is: same retry classifier, same backoff shape, and same defaults. Also same env var names for auth.

[17:52] Priya Natarajan: What env var name?

[17:55] Ibrahim Khan: Redwood API key env var. Today some clients use slightly different names; we’re consolidating. I’ll send the doc after.

[18:04] Priya Natarajan: Great.

[18:06] Sarah Kim: Do you have an example of “safe retries”? Like, do you retry POSTs? Some libraries only retry GET.

[18:14] Ibrahim Khan: We do retry POSTs for these API calls because the API is “request-response” and we treat it like RPC. But we put strict limits. Also we do not retry on 4xx besides 429.

[18:28] Dana Lo: And we won’t retry on validation errors obviously.

[18:32] Miguel Alvarez: What about 408 request timeout?

[18:35] Ibrahim Khan: We treat some 408s as retryable, but it depends if it’s from our gateway vs an intermediary. The general rule: if it’s clearly a transient network/gateway condition, yes. But again, limited attempts.

[18:51] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[18:53] Nikhil Sharma: If it helps, we can also share recommended metrics: count retries, retry reason, and total attempts so you can see if you’re amplifying.

[19:02] Miguel Alvarez: That would be helpful. We use Datadog.

[19:05] Ibrahim Khan: Perfect. We have a telemetry hook design. It’s optional, but we can give you a way to emit a callback on each retry attempt.

[19:18] Sarah Kim: Nice.

[19:20] Priya Natarajan: But make sure the telemetry doesn’t include prompt text.

[19:23] Ibrahim Khan: Agreed.

[19:25] Dana Lo: On the streaming parsing side, can you confirm if you’re seeing “event:” lines or only “data:”?

[19:32] Sarah Kim: Mostly data. Sometimes we saw “event: message” I think.

[19:38] Dana Lo: We use event types for some frames (like “error” or “done”). But again, some proxies strip or merge lines. The parser should handle unknown events.

[19:50] Miguel Alvarez: We also saw “retry: 5000” once.

[19:54] Dana Lo: That’s an SSE field but we shouldn’t be sending that, I think. Might be from some intermediate? Or a misread from the logger.

[20:02] Sarah Kim: Could be.

[20:04] Ibrahim Khan: The important part is the framing. Each event ends with double newline. The SDK should be tolerant.

[20:12] Nikhil Sharma: Okay, let’s land a plan. I think first, you disable compression on your SSE route and make sure proxy buffering is off. Second, send us a repro snippet and request IDs.

[20:26] Miguel Alvarez: Works.

[20:28] Sarah Kim: Can you also tell us the “right” way to do cancellation? Like if the user closes the browser, we should cancel upstream.

[20:36] Dana Lo: Yes. You should wire browser disconnect to AbortController, and the SDK should send the abort to fetch, and close the stream cleanly.

[20:47] Sarah Kim: Today we aren’t doing that. So maybe upstream keeps running.

[20:51] Nikhil Sharma: That could also cause weirdness and wasted tokens.

[20:55] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. Also, cancellation should not be retried. Another parity rule.

[21:02] Sarah Kim: Makes sense.

[21:04] Priya Natarajan: I have one more security question. Do you support restricting keys by environment or IP?

[21:10] Nikhil Sharma: We have scoped keys and org/project separation. IP allowlisting depends on the plan; we can follow up with your security requirements. But for the SDK specifically, it’s just using the key in the Authorization header.

[21:25] Priya Natarajan: Okay.

[21:27] Miguel Alvarez: Can I ask: do other customers do streaming behind Cloudflare without issues?

[21:32] Nikhil Sharma: Yes, but they usually have to tweak buffering settings and timeouts. It’s a known “gotcha” with SSE.

[21:41] Dana Lo: And making sure there are periodic flushes.

[21:44] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[21:46] Ibrahim Khan: For the disconnect you saw at ~60 seconds, I strongly suspect an idle timeout. Because it’s a round number. But the duplicate request IDs suggest an intermediary retry.

[21:58] Miguel Alvarez: Envoy does retries on certain reset reasons. I’ll check our config.

[22:04] Dana Lo: If Envoy retries, you might want to disable retries for that route, at least for streaming. Or set it to retry only on connect-failure before any bytes.

[22:15] Miguel Alvarez: Right. We can do that.

[22:18] Sarah Kim: What about Redwood side—do you ever disconnect streams? Like do you have a max duration?

[22:24] Nikhil Sharma: There is a max request duration on the gateway, but it’s generous. If you’re hitting it, you’d see a specific error. But the short disconnects you describe don’t sound like that.

[22:37] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[22:38] Ibrahim Khan: If you can send us one request-id where you got disconnected, we can check if we closed it or the client did.

[22:46] Sarah Kim: Got it.

[22:48] Nikhil Sharma: We’re at about the halfway mark. Any other questions on the retry spec you need, to evaluate us?

[22:56] Miguel Alvarez: I think the main thing is: we don’t want “infinite” retries and we want jitter. And we want to respect Retry-After.

[23:04] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, agreed. No infinite. We also want “retry budget” to avoid synchronized storms.

[23:12] Sarah Kim: Is it configurable? Like can we set max retries = 0?

[23:16] Dana Lo: Yes. The plan is: global defaults, plus per-request override. And you can disable retries entirely.

[23:24] Sarah Kim: Great.

[23:26] Priya Natarajan: And you’ll document it. Because enterprise reviewers will ask.

[23:30] Nikhil Sharma: Yes. We’re updating docs and quickstarts.

[23:34] Dana Lo: Also we’ll standardize error messages so it’s clear what happened.

[23:40] Sarah Kim: Cool.

[23:42] Miguel Alvarez: Okay, can we talk about the “best practice” if we really need automatic resume? Like are you considering it?

[23:49] Nikhil Sharma: Not in the immediate roadmap. It requires server-side support (event IDs, deterministic replay). For now, the app pattern is: detect disconnect, and either show an error or restart from scratch with a user-visible notice.

[24:06] Ibrahim Khan: One thing some customers do is they save the conversation state and reissue with the prior messages plus “continue from here” instruction. But you still risk different text.

[24:18] Sarah Kim: Yeah we can do that.

[24:20] Dana Lo: But again, don’t do it silently.

[24:22] Sarah Kim: Understood.

[24:25] (crosstalk)

[24:26] Miguel Alvarez: Sorry go ahead.

[24:27] Dana Lo: No you go.

[24:28] Miguel Alvarez: I was going to say, we also benchmarked with OpenAI streaming and didn’t see disconnects, but their tokens start faster.

[24:37] Nikhil Sharma: That’s fair. Different models have different TTFT. We can help you pick models that are faster to first token if that matters.

[24:47] Sarah Kim: It does. If first token takes 40 seconds, our proxy will kill it.

[24:52] Ibrahim Khan: Then you have two levers: (1) increase the proxy’s “upstream idle” and “request timeout”, (2) choose a model that returns first token faster.

[25:05] Dana Lo: Also enabling streaming properly with flush can prevent “no bytes” for too long.

[25:12] Miguel Alvarez: Okay.

[25:13] Priya Natarajan: You mentioned API keys from env vars. Do you support reading keys from files? Some orgs mount secrets as files.

[25:20] Ibrahim Khan: We’re discussing it. Security tends to prefer env vars or explicit injection through config, but file-based secrets can be okay if done carefully. Our default is env var + explicit parameter.

[25:32] Priya Natarajan: Okay.

[25:34] Nikhil Sharma: We can follow up with our security guidance doc. But for now, in your k8s, env vars from secrets is common.

[25:43] Priya Natarajan: Yep.

[25:45] Sarah Kim: One more: When the stream disconnects, does the SDK throw immediately, or can it hang?

[25:51] Dana Lo: It should throw. If it hangs, that’s a bug. Sometimes sockets close and you don’t get an event. That’s why timeouts matter.

[26:01] Sarah Kim: We did see a hang in Python once.

[26:04] Ibrahim Khan: That’s actually one of the issues we’re fixing in Python: read timeout behavior + streaming parsing. So yes, known.

[26:14] Miguel Alvarez: Good to know.

[26:16] Nikhil Sharma: Okay, I think we’ve got enough to proceed. Let’s do a recap.

[26:21] Nikhil Sharma: Sarah/Miguel: you’ll disable gzip/compression on SSE route, verify Envoy retry policy for the Redwood upstream, and send us a repro with request IDs.

[26:32] Miguel Alvarez: Yep.

[26:34] Sarah Kim: Yep.

[26:35] Nikhil Sharma: Redwood side: Dana will check the TS SDK version behavior, especially around any implicit retries on streaming and error mapping. Ibrahim will send our guidance on retries/timeouts/streaming and recommended app patterns.

[26:49] Dana Lo: Yes.

[26:50] Ibrahim Khan: Yep.

[26:52] Priya Natarajan: And please include the note about logging redaction and which headers are required.

[26:57] Ibrahim Khan: Will do.

[27:00] Nikhil Sharma: Great. We’ll schedule a follow-up early next week.

[27:05] Sarah Kim: Thanks.

[27:06] Miguel Alvarez: Thanks all.

[27:08] Priya Natarajan: Thank you.

[27:10] (meeting ends — recording continued with silence)
